chapter: The French Revolution: Ideas, the Estates General and the Republic
trick: Hold on to three dates and the whole chapter lines up. 1614 — the last time the Estates General met. 1789 — Louis XVI is forced to recall it because the treasury is empty, 175 years later. 1792 — the monarchy is abolished and the First Republic proclaimed. Between the second and third date sit the thinkers who made it thinkable: Rousseau above all, whose General Will said sovereignty belongs to the people, and the Jacobins under Robespierre who acted on that idea to the letter.

chapter: Napoleon: Rise, the Code and the Fall
trick: Read Napoleon in three movements and the questions sort themselves. RISE — 1799, the coup of 18 Brumaire, planned from inside the Directory by Sieyès, who meant to use Napoleon and was used instead. REFORM — 1800, the Bank of France; 1804, the Code Napoléon, one law for the whole country in place of a tangle of local custom, which Lefebvre called the Bible of French society. FALL — 1813, Leipzig, the Battle of Nations, where four powers at once finally broke him, two years before Waterloo finished it.

chapter: The Atmosphere: Composition, Layers and Weather Instruments
trick: Two lists and one rule carry this chapter. The layers from the ground up: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere — weather in the first because that is where the water vapour is, ozone in the second. The composition: nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, argon about 1%, carbon dioxide a trace — nearly four-fifths of the air is the gas you do not breathe for respiration. The rule: wind always blows from high pressure to low, never the other way. Then match each instrument to its quantity — barometer to pressure, rain gauge to rainfall, anemometer to wind speed, hygrometer to humidity.

chapter: The Hydrosphere: Oceans, the Water Cycle and Tides
trick: The hydrosphere means all the water on Earth — not the oceans alone, which is the trap in almost every question on it. About 71% of the surface is under water, and the Pacific alone covers roughly a third of the planet, more than all the land put together. The water cycle turns endlessly through evaporation, condensation, precipitation and run-off; condensation is the stage that makes cloud, and it is simply evaporation run backwards. Tides come mainly from the Moon: far smaller than the Sun but far closer, and tidal pull falls away sharply with distance.

items.statement: The hydrosphere means the oceans and nothing else.
items.why: It is all the water on Earth — oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, ice and the vapour in the air. Naming only one part is the commonest mistake on this chapter.

items.statement: About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water.
items.why: Which leaves roughly 29% as land, and is why it is called the blue planet.

items.statement: The Atlantic is the largest ocean.
items.why: The Pacific is, by a wide margin — about a third of the Earth's surface. The Atlantic is second.

items.statement: Condensation turns water vapour back into liquid droplets.
items.why: It is evaporation run backwards, and it is the stage that forms cloud, mist and dew.

items.statement: Tides are caused mainly by the Sun.
items.why: Mainly by the Moon. The Sun is far larger but far further away, and tidal pull falls off sharply with distance, so the Moon's effect is about twice the Sun's.

items.statement: The Bay of Bengal is part of the Indian Ocean.
items.why: Its north-eastern arm, between India and Myanmar — the largest bay in the world.
